summary: Comments from UCLA-CCN on the proposed Data Transfer Protocol and File Transfer Protocol. They say separators in one DTP mode need sequence numbers, the modes-available handshake should not be mandatory, and in FTP ending a file by closing the connection should signal an error, not a normal end.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC reviews proposed data and file transfer rules and points out cases that could confuse users or servers. It suggests clearer markers for transfer boundaries and errors.

subtitle: Comments on design issues in proposed Data Transfer and File Transfer Protocols.

tldr.problem: The proposals for DTP and FTP left questions about restart markers, mode negotiation, end-of-file signals, and file storage commands.
tldr.mechanism: R. T. Braden lists specific changes, including sequence numbers for information separators, an optional modes-available exchange, and a separate file separator for normal completion.
tldr.outcome: RFC 238 updates RFCs 171 and 172 with comments for the protocol designers; it does not specify a final replacement.

sections.title: Reviewing DTP and FTP
sections.content:
R. T. Braden of UCLA-CCN comments on proposals for the Data Transfer Protocol and File Transfer Protocol. The note updates RFCs 171 and 172 by identifying issues for the protocol designers to consider.

The comments cover both the transfer of data and the commands used to store and retrieve files.
sections.plainLanguage: The author reads draft rules for moving data and files. He lists details that could lead to uncertainty during a transfer.

sections.title: Separators and Mode Negotiation
sections.content:
For Descriptor/Count mode, Braden recommends adding a transaction sequence number to Information Separators so the receiver can tell whether all transactions before the separator arrived. He says separate separator forms are needed for Descriptor/Count and DLE modes.

He also argues that the modes-available handshake should not be mandatory. A receiver can learn which mode the transmitter uses from the first data or control transaction.
sections.plainLanguage: A separator should carry enough information to show where it belongs in the transfer. The author also questions making both sides list possible modes before sending begins.

sections.title: File Completion and Requests
sections.content:
The RFC says closing a connection without a File Separator should mean an error or aborted transfer, not normal end-of-file. Otherwise, the receiver cannot tell a completed transfer from a sender that failed.

Other suggestions include separate store requests for creating or replacing a file, allowing service hosts to require user names and passwords, and including explanatory text with error codes.
sections.plainLanguage: A normal file ending needs an explicit signal. A connection that simply closes should warn the receiver that something may have gone wrong.
